beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. When I first heard about loop engineering, my honest first thought was, wouldn't this cost me way more tokens, and more money? Fair question. But it turns out that isn't the question that decides whether a loop is worth building. Let's open it up.

props.segment: Loops That Know When to Stop
props.command: Everyone's talking about 'loop engineering' — building a system that prompts the AI for me instead of me prompting it turn by turn. Won't that just burn way more tokens? When is it actually worth it?
output: yes — loops cost more per task
the real test: time saved, not cost
worth it only if it can verify itself

beats.narration_text: So what is a loop? Instead of prompting the AI turn by turn, you build a system that prompts it for you. It triggers itself, runs, checks its own work, and decides the next step, with no human in each run. Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code, says his job now is writing loops.

show.event: a loop arc begins; the TRIGGER node lights
the RUN node lights along the arc
the arc closes back to the start — no human node in the ring

layers.title: decides the next step
layers.sub: no human in the loop each run

props.caption: a system that prompts the AI for you — Cherny: “writing loops”

beats.narration_text: Here's the reframe. Yes, loops cost more per task than a single prompt, repeated context, extra tool calls, iteration. But that's the wrong place to stop. The real question isn't what a loop costs, it's whether it saves you enough time to be worth it.

show.event: the 'cost per task' question strikes through
the 'time saved' question types in beneath (accent)
a small 'reportedly' stat line settles under the chips

items: ✓  right question — hours of your time saved
props.caption: the cost is real — the question is what it saves

beats.narration_text: Before you build one, two things have to be true. First, a clear trigger, a schedule, a GitHub event, a file change. Second, a verifiable exit condition, tests passing, a metric clearing, or a human approving. Miss the trigger and it never runs. Miss the exit and it never stops.

show.event: the TRIGGER layer stacks in with its examples

show.at: never runs. Miss the exit and it never stops
show.event: a red 'never runs / never stops' caption resolves

layers.title: a clear TRIGGER
layers.sub: schedule · GitHub event · API call · file change

layers.title: a verifiable EXIT
layers.sub: tests pass · metric clears · human approves

layers.title: miss either →
layers.sub: it never runs, or it never stops

beats.narration_text: That's the sweet spot, repetitive, well-defined, high-volume work. Nightly refactors. Babysitting pull-request reviews and tests. Reconciling invoices or data. Overnight code you review with your morning coffee. Clear task, repeats often, easy to check.

show.event: four use-case chips light in narration order

items: overnight code you review at dawn
props.caption: repetitive · well-defined · high-volume

beats.narration_text: And where do loops quietly blow up? One-off, judgment-heavy work. Anything with no reliable way to check success. And high-frequency runs with no caps, agents stuck retrying forever, burning real money. Looking busy is not the same as being done.

show.event: the first anti-pattern layer stacks in
the 'stuck retrying, burning $' layer stacks in (accent)

props.caption: busy is not the same as done

beats.narration_text: If you do build one, keep the cost sane. Cap iterations, time, and spend. Use cheap models to generate, strong ones to verify. Externalize the context you repeat into skills or caching. And prefer deterministic checks, tests and linters, over the AI grading itself.

show.event: four habit chips light in narration order

items: cheap to generate, strong to verify
props.caption: four habits that keep loops affordable

beats.narration_text: So here's the whole thing on one page. Loop engineering isn't a free upgrade, it's infrastructure. Before you build, ask: is there a trigger and a stop condition? Can verification run on its own? Does it repeat enough to earn the setup? If yes, build it. If no, a plain prompt still wins.

artifactLines: It has a clear trigger AND a verifiable stop condition — or it never runs, or never stops.
Verification can run mostly on its own: tests, linters, thresholds — not the AI grading itself.
The work repeats often and at enough volume to earn the setup cost.
Caps on iterations, time, and spend are in place — otherwise it just burns tokens while looking productive.

beats.narration_text: That's the short version. The full video also covers Let's run a real task… and loops that know when to stop — watch Loops That Know When to Stop. for the whole story. The link is right below.
